classification.difficultyReason: Uses restricted lattice paths and partitions routes at a diagonal to prove counting identities.

content.prompt:
The diagram shows a $6\times4$ grid. The aim is to walk from point A to point B by walking along the black lines either downwards or to the right.

A single move is defined as walking along one side of a single small square, thus it always takes you ten moves to get from A to B.

By treating paths as ordered sequences of D and R:

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find how many different routes are possible:

spec.description: Four columns and six rows of square cells; labelled endpoint dots. Labels and point markers require TikZ rather than the blank-grid template.
spec.mathematics: Every route contains six D moves and four R moves.

answer.worked:
Arrange six Ds and four Rs. Choose the six positions occupied by D; the remaining positions contain R.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{10!}{6!4!}&={}^{10}C_6\\&=210\end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, choose the four R positions: ${}^{10}C_4={}^{10}C_6$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: if you must pass through C,

spec.description: Four-column, six-row grid with C two columns right and two rows down from A. Labelled points require TikZ.
spec.mathematics: A to C uses two D and two R moves; C to B uses four D and two R moves.

answer.worked:
From A to C, arrange two Ds and two Rs. From C to B, arrange four Ds and two Rs. The two route choices are independent.
$$\begin{aligned}N&={}^{4}C_2\times{}^{6}C_4\\&=6\times15\\&=90\end{aligned}$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: if you cannot move along the top line of the grid,

answer.worked:
The first move must be D. Arrange the remaining five Ds and four Rs in nine positions.
$$\begin{aligned}N&={}^{9}C_5\\&=126\end{aligned}$$

children.label: iv
children.prompt: if you cannot move along the second row from the top of the grid.

answer.worked:
No R move is allowed on the horizontal grid line one square below the top. Therefore the first two D moves must be consecutive.

Treat DD as one object. Arrange this object with the remaining four Ds and four Rs, with DD first among the five downward objects. Choose the four R positions among the nine objects; the downward objects then have a unique order.
$$\begin{aligned}N&={}^{9}C_4\\&=126\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Notice that every route must pass through one and only one of the five crossed points.

This is because a path must cross a diagonal to get from A to B.

Hence prove that
$$\begin{aligned}{}^{10}C_4={}&{}^{4}C_0\times{}^{6}C_4+{}^{4}C_1\times{}^{6}C_3\\&+{}^{4}C_2\times{}^{6}C_2+{}^{4}C_3\times{}^{6}C_1\\&+{}^{4}C_4\times{}^{6}C_0.\end{aligned}$$

spec.description: Five crosses on the fourth-move diagonal of a four-column, six-row grid; no joining diagonal is drawn. C is the central crossed point.
spec.mathematics: Crossed vertices have rightward-plus-downward coordinates summing to four.

answer.short: Partition all ${}^{10}C_4$ routes by their unique crossed point. The five case counts are ${}^{4}C_k{}^{6}C_{4-k}$ for $k=0,1,2,3,4$; adding proves the identity.
answer.worked:
There are ${}^{10}C_4$ routes in total. Each move increases the sum of the rightward and downward coordinates by one, so every route reaches exactly one crossed point after four moves.

For the crossed point reached using $k$ R moves, the first four moves contain $k$ Rs and $4-k$ Ds. There are ${}^{4}C_k$ ways to reach it. The remaining six moves contain $4-k$ Rs and $2+k$ Ds, giving ${}^{6}C_{4-k}$ ways to finish.

From left to right, the five case counts are
$$\begin{aligned}k=0:&\quad{}^{4}C_0\times{}^{6}C_4,\\k=1:&\quad{}^{4}C_1\times{}^{6}C_3,\\k=2:&\quad{}^{4}C_2\times{}^{6}C_2,\\k=3:&\quad{}^{4}C_3\times{}^{6}C_1,\\k=4:&\quad{}^{4}C_4\times{}^{6}C_0.\end{aligned}$$
These cases are disjoint and include every route, so their sum equals ${}^{10}C_4$, as required.

children.label: c
children.prompt:
What diagonal would you draw to prove that
$$\begin{aligned}{}^{10}C_4={}&{}^{5}C_0\times{}^{5}C_4+{}^{5}C_1\times{}^{5}C_3\\&+{}^{5}C_2\times{}^{5}C_2+{}^{5}C_3\times{}^{5}C_1\\&+{}^{5}C_4\times{}^{5}C_0?\end{aligned}$$

answer.short: Use the diagonal through the vertices reached after five moves: $(0,5),(1,4),(2,3),(3,2),(4,1)$, measured rightwards and downwards from A.
answer.worked:
Mark the five grid vertices reached after five moves: $(0,5),(1,4),(2,3),(3,2),(4,1)$, where coordinates count moves right and down from A. They lie on the diagonal $x+y=5$.

A route passing through the point with $k$ R moves in its first five moves can be chosen in ${}^{5}C_k{}^{5}C_{4-k}$ ways. Every route meets exactly one of these points, so adding the five cases gives the stated identity.

children.label: d
children.prompt:
Using the $6\times6$ grid, then using the same idea as that used in parts b and c, prove that
$$\begin{aligned}{}^{12}C_6={}&({}^{6}C_0)^2+({}^{6}C_1)^2+({}^{6}C_2)^2\\&+({}^{6}C_3)^2+({}^{6}C_4)^2+({}^{6}C_5)^2\\&+({}^{6}C_6)^2.\end{aligned}$$

answer.short: Partition the ${}^{12}C_6$ routes by the point reached after six moves. The seven case counts are $({}^{6}C_k)^2$, for $k=0,1,\ldots,6$, giving the identity.
answer.worked:
There are ${}^{12}C_6$ routes from A to B: arrange six Ds and six Rs.

Every route passes through exactly one of the seven marked vertices after six moves. If the first six moves contain $k$ Rs, they contain $6-k$ Ds and can be arranged in ${}^{6}C_k$ ways. The last six moves then contain $6-k$ Rs and $k$ Ds, and can be arranged in ${}^{6}C_{6-k}={}^{6}C_k$ ways.

Thus the number of routes through that vertex is $({}^{6}C_k)^2$. Adding the seven disjoint cases gives
$$\begin{aligned}{}^{12}C_6&=\sum_{k=0}^{6}({}^{6}C_k)^2\\&=1+36+225+400+225+36+1\\&=924.\end{aligned}$$
